```{r}
#| label: load-packages
#| include: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(janitor)
library(tidymodels)
library(xgboost)
library(probably)
```

## Introduction

We will extend the evaluation framework from class using the white wine quality
data. You will fit three classifiers, compare them using ROC and precision-recall
curves, explore the effect of the classification threshold, and assess probability
calibration.

```{r}
fd <- read.csv("~/Desktop/School/Current Classes/INFO_3200/data/winequality-white.csv", sep = ";") |>
  clean_names() |>
  mutate(quality_wine = as.factor(ifelse(quality >= 7, "High", "Low")))
```

1. Split the data into training (80%) and testing (20%) samples. Check the
class balance in the test set. What fraction of wines are "High" quality?
Why does this matter for model evaluation?

```{r}
set.seed(8675309)

split <- initial_split(fd, prop = 0.80, strata = quality_wine)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

# Class balance in test set
test |>
  count(quality_wine) |>
  mutate(fraction = n / sum(n))

# About 22% of wines are "High" quality — the classes are imbalanced.
# This matters because accuracy alone is misleading: a model that always
# predicts "Low" would still be ~78% accurate. Metrics like ROC AUC,
# PR AUC, and the choice of threshold all need to account for this imbalance.
```

2. Fit the following three classifiers on the training data and obtain
probability predictions on the test set using `augment()`:
  a. Logistic regression (`logistic_reg()`)
  b. Random forest (`rand_forest(mtry = 4, trees = 500)` with `set_engine("ranger", probability = TRUE)`)
  c. Gradient boosted classifier (`boost_tree(trees = 500, tree_depth = 3, learn_rate = 0.05)`)

```{r}
#| cache: true

rec <- recipe(quality_wine ~ ., data = train) |>
  step_rm(quality) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

# --- Logistic Regression ---
lr_spec <- logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm")
lr_wf   <- workflow() |> add_recipe(rec) |> add_model(lr_spec)
lr_fit  <- fit(lr_wf, data = train)
lr_preds <- augment(lr_fit, new_data = test)

# --- Random Forest ---
rf_spec <- rand_forest(mtry = 4, trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", probability = TRUE) |>
  set_mode("classification")
rf_wf   <- workflow() |> add_recipe(rec) |> add_model(rf_spec)
rf_fit  <- fit(rf_wf, data = train)
rf_preds <- augment(rf_fit, new_data = test)

# --- Gradient Boosted Trees ---
xgb_spec <- boost_tree(trees = 500, tree_depth = 3, learn_rate = 0.05) |>
  set_engine("xgboost") |>
  set_mode("classification")
xgb_wf   <- workflow() |> add_recipe(rec) |> add_model(xgb_spec)
xgb_fit  <- fit(xgb_wf, data = train)
xgb_preds <- augment(xgb_fit, new_data = test)
```

3. Plot all three ROC curves on the same figure using `ggplot2`. Which model
dominates? Is there a region of the curve (low FPR vs. high FPR) where one
model is clearly superior to the others?

```{r}
# Build ROC curve data for each model
roc_lr  <- roc_curve(lr_preds,  truth = quality_wine, .pred_High) |> mutate(model = "Logistic Regression")
roc_rf  <- roc_curve(rf_preds,  truth = quality_wine, .pred_High) |> mutate(model = "Random Forest")
roc_xgb <- roc_curve(xgb_preds, truth = quality_wine, .pred_High) |> mutate(model = "XGBoost")

roc_all <- bind_rows(roc_lr, roc_rf, roc_xgb)

ggplot(roc_all, aes(x = 1 - specificity, y = sensitivity, color = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("steelblue", "darkorange", "forestgreen")) +
  labs(
    title = "ROC Curves — Three Classifiers",
    x = "False Positive Rate (1 − Specificity)",
    y = "True Positive Rate (Sensitivity)",
    color = "Model"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# XGBoost and Random Forest generally dominate Logistic Regression.
# At low FPR (< 0.1) — where precision matters most — XGBoost tends to
# pull ahead slightly. At higher FPR, all three converge. Logistic
# regression lags across most of the curve.
```

4. Compute ROC AUC and PR AUC for all three models. Arrange the results in a
single table. Do the two metrics agree on which model is best? If not, which
metric is more appropriate here and why?

```{r}
compute_metrics <- function(preds, model_name) {
  bind_rows(
    roc_auc(preds, truth = quality_wine, .pred_High) |> mutate(metric = "ROC AUC"),
    pr_auc(preds,  truth = quality_wine, .pred_High) |> mutate(metric = "PR AUC")
  ) |>
    select(metric, .estimate) |>
    mutate(model = model_name)
}

metrics_table <- bind_rows(
  compute_metrics(lr_preds,  "Logistic Regression"),
  compute_metrics(rf_preds,  "Random Forest"),
  compute_metrics(xgb_preds, "XGBoost")
) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = metric, values_from = .estimate) |>
  arrange(desc(`ROC AUC`))

metrics_table

# Both metrics typically agree that tree-based models outperform logistic
# regression. Given the class imbalance (~22% High), PR AUC is the more
# informative metric: it focuses on the minority class and is more sensitive
# to how well the model identifies "High" quality wines without flooding
# predictions with false positives.
```

5. Using the gradient boosted model's predictions, find the probability threshold
that maximises Youden's J statistic (sensitivity + specificity − 1). Apply that
threshold to generate a new predicted class column and compare the resulting
confusion matrix to the default 0.5 threshold. What changed?

```{r}
# Build full ROC curve for XGBoost
roc_xgb_full <- roc_curve(xgb_preds, truth = quality_wine, .pred_High)

# Youden's J = sensitivity + specificity - 1
best_thresh <- roc_xgb_full |>
  mutate(j_stat = sensitivity + specificity - 1) |>
  slice_max(j_stat, n = 1)

best_thresh

youden_threshold <- best_thresh$.threshold

# Default 0.5 confusion matrix
xgb_preds |>
  mutate(.pred_class_05 = factor(ifelse(.pred_High >= 0.5, "High", "Low"),
                                  levels = c("High", "Low"))) |>
  conf_mat(truth = quality_wine, estimate = .pred_class_05)

# Youden's J threshold confusion matrix
xgb_preds |>
  mutate(.pred_class_youden = factor(ifelse(.pred_High >= youden_threshold, "High", "Low"),
                                      levels = c("High", "Low"))) |>
  conf_mat(truth = quality_wine, estimate = .pred_class_youden)

# The Youden threshold is typically lower than 0.5 for an imbalanced dataset.
# This recovers more true "High" quality wines (higher sensitivity / recall)
# at the cost of more false positives. The default 0.5 is overly conservative
# and misses many positives in this imbalanced setting.
```

6. Suppose the cost of a missed "High" quality wine (false negative) is five
times the cost of a false alarm (false positive). Using the precision-recall
curve and/or the ROC curve, identify a threshold that reflects this cost
asymmetry. Justify your choice.

```{r}
# Cost-sensitive threshold: cost_FN = 5 * cost_FP
# On the ROC curve, the optimal slope = (cost_FP / cost_FN) * (N_neg / N_pos)
# = (1/5) * (n_Low / n_High)

n_high <- sum(test$quality_wine == "High")
n_low  <- sum(test$quality_wine == "Low")
cost_ratio <- (1 / 5) * (n_low / n_high)

# Find threshold where ROC slope ≈ cost_ratio
# Approximate by finding where (Δsensitivity / Δspecificity) is closest to cost_ratio
roc_cost <- roc_xgb_full |>
  mutate(
    d_sens = c(diff(sensitivity), NA),
    d_spec = c(diff(specificity), NA),
    slope  = abs(d_sens / d_spec)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(slope)) |>
  mutate(diff_from_target = abs(slope - cost_ratio)) |>
  slice_min(diff_from_target, n = 1)

cost_threshold <- roc_cost$.threshold
cat("Cost-sensitive threshold:", round(cost_threshold, 4), "\n")

# Apply it and check recall
xgb_preds |>
  mutate(.pred_cost = factor(ifelse(.pred_High >= cost_threshold, "High", "Low"),
                              levels = c("High", "Low"))) |>
  conf_mat(truth = quality_wine, estimate = .pred_cost)

# Because false negatives are 5x more costly, we set a lower classification
# threshold than the default 0.5. This shifts the operating point on the ROC
# curve toward higher sensitivity, accepting more false positives to ensure
# "High" quality wines are rarely missed. The cost ratio determines the
# exact slope at which the optimal point lies on the ROC curve.
```

7. Plot calibration curves (`cal_plot_breaks()` from the `probably` package)
for all three models. Which model is best calibrated? Does the best-calibrated
model also have the highest AUC?

```{r}
# probably expects a two_class_pred or tibble with truth + predicted probabilities
# cal_plot_breaks works directly on augmented tibbles

p_lr <- cal_plot_breaks(lr_preds,  truth = quality_wine, estimate = .pred_High) +
  ggtitle("Logistic Regression") + theme_minimal()

p_rf <- cal_plot_breaks(rf_preds,  truth = quality_wine, estimate = .pred_High) +
  ggtitle("Random Forest") + theme_minimal()

p_xgb <- cal_plot_breaks(xgb_preds, truth = quality_wine, estimate = .pred_High) +
  ggtitle("XGBoost") + theme_minimal()

library(patchwork)
p_lr | p_rf | p_xgb

# Logistic regression is typically the best-calibrated of the three —
# its predicted probabilities more closely follow the diagonal (perfect
# calibration). Tree-based models like random forests and gradient boosters
# are known to produce overconfident or poorly-spread probability estimates.
# It is common for the best-calibrated model to NOT have the highest AUC:
# calibration and discrimination are separate properties. A model can rank
# cases well (high AUC) while still mis-stating actual probabilities.
```
